chunks: And what Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Abdullah ibn Maymun al-Qaddah, from Ja'far, from his father (peace be upon them both), that Ali (peace be upon him) used to say:
"Whoever misses fasting the three days in Hajj, which are the day before Tarwiyah, the day of Tarwiyah, and the day of Arafah, let him fast the days of Tashriq, for he has been permitted [to do so]."
These two reports came as singular (shadh) contrary to all other reports, and it is not permissible to rely on them and depart from the multitude of hadiths except by a way that removes the excuse.

It is possible that the two men erred regarding Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) in that, and that they had heard it from someone else among those attributed to the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon them).
Because it has been narrated that this was said by Abdullah ibn al-Hasan, and they attributed it to him by error.
And even if they were safe from that, acting upon them would not be obligatory, because the preceding reports narrated from him had opposed these two reports and exceeded them in number.

And if they were all equal so that there was no distinction between them, it would be obligatory to discard acting upon all of them and to rely on what Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) narrated from his father (peace be upon him).
Because his narration (peace be upon him) has an apparent distinction over the narration of others due to his infallibility, purity, chastity, and freedom from error.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for missing the three days of fasting during Hajj according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* analyzes the validity of compensating for missed Hajj fasting days by fasting during Tashriq, noting that the report is *shadh* (singular) and contradicts the majority of narrations. The scholar emphasizes that even if accepted, the narration of Imam Musa ibn Ja'far is preferred due to his infallibility (*ismah*) and freedom from error, a key principle in Shia jurisprudence for resolving conflicting reports. It also suggests the possibility of human error (*wahm*) in the transmission chain, highlighting the rigorous scrutiny applied to hadith authenticity.
